title: The hardest part of my AI text RPG wasn't the writing, it was getting the model to stop inventing state
author: No-Pollution7797
selftext:
I've been building a text RPG where an LLM narrates every turn, on the side. When I started I assumed the hard part would be prose quality. It wasn't. The model writes fine. The real problem was that it kept quietly changing the world: an NPC who died two sessions ago shows up at the tavern, the player "remembers" a key they never picked up, a faction that hated you is suddenly friendly.

What helped most was splitting the job in two. One step decides what actually happened and writes it to saved state, and the narration step only gets to describe that. It can't add items or bring people back. That one change fixed more than any amount of prompt tweaking did.

The part I still haven't solved is old stuff. Things the player set up early but never came back to either crowd the context forever or drop out and get forgotten, and neither feels right.

For people doing long-running AI games: how do you decide what the model still needs to see after 50+ turns?

comments.author: DrinkingAtQuarks
comments.body:
Seems like a multi agent approach would be beneficial. Ie having a specific agent that checks for continuity in the script that is distinct from the writing agent. 

Also a context window as large as possible to ensure as much of the previous text as possible preempts any output.

Could also consider a custom file format (like a .md or .html) that keeps track of immutable things like inventory/character states at any given timepoint. 

Interesting problem to solve, even if AI makes the coding/writing easy.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: A separate checker is roughly where I ended up, though it worked better for me when it decides what happened first instead of reviewing the prose afterwards. A bigger context helped less than I hoped, the model still skims right past old details.

comments.author: HuWeiliu
comments.body:
For any particular state you could generate relevant wordings. I.e. in which context it becomes relevant again. Add those as embeddings, and for each event, search embeddings for stuff that isn't already in the context and add it in, maybe with a limit by relevance.

AI deciding which plot points are interesting etc and doing a good job is probably another issue you are facing I assume. I haven't had good success with it writing interesting stories

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Writing down when something would matter again at save time is a nice idea, that's exactly what plain similarity search misses. And yeah, getting it to pick which threads are actually interesting is its own fight.

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body: I don't understand the economics of using an LLM in a game. Say a player uses 50c worth of tokens in an hour of playing. Then if they play for 10 hours, you're out $5, probably erasing any profit you made from sale of the game.

replies.author: Marod_
replies.body: That use case should be simple enough for a local LMM to handle though.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: It's a real constraint. It's a big part of why most of these end up as subscriptions or pay per play rather than a one-time purchase.

replies.author: Robonotes1760
replies.body: Surely BYOK is the answer?

replies.author: SassyTextDev
replies.body:
DeepSeek4.1-flash

You can absolutely make it work but it has to run on deepseek, and you have to heavily use input cache.

replies.author: OWazabi
replies.body:
You can make that run locally, you don't run it through your API tokens obviously.  
Fine tunes go a huge way, people HUGELY underestimate how good a small model can be if it is properly fine tuned to a specific use case.

comments.author: blackskies69
comments.body: AI text RPG's are a fantasy you'll never reproduce a reliable experience. People have been trying to do this with sillytavern for years and its still janky.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Fair, jank is the default. I'm mostly curious how far it goes once the bookkeeping lives outside the model and it only has to write.

replies.author: SassyTextDev
replies.body:
I've been building literally this for months. I think I'm close. I'd send you a link but I'm still a new account and I don't want to get fucked. I can *dm* you a link.

It's the hardest fucking thing I've ever tried to build, but I think it can be done.

The object permanence requires a DB storage solution which requires a node tree solution. GM can't remember the tavern owner because it was 50 turns ago. But if you have the character sheet of that guy, and can load it *when the player returns to the tavern*, then yeah, put it top of mind and the model gets it.

It's SO FUCKING HARD. I uh... made 5 videos about it?

It can be done.

https://i.redd.it/82agnh86zz0i1.png

Has to run on deepseek or some cheap-as-balls MOE model. And you have to split up responsibility between GM and like 10 other brains. A single model can say "I need an image of a place that looks like this" but that has to delegate to a subagent that reads the charter on "ok here's how to image prompt without it looking like balls". That time 10. Time 20. FUck... uhh Times however many "brains" I'm up to now

replies.author: blackskies69
replies.body: Right, but then you're asking a player to bring a model into your game. Models that change, and you're hoping that an average user will know how to use an API. If you try to switch to local models then you run into hardware limitations. How are you handling all of that?

replies.author: SassyTextDev
replies.body:
Nah man, product. Website. Sign up, give me money, I wrote the stuff.

The GM is the main brain. It responds with an array of tool calls, some of which delegate to other brains. It only worries about writing interesting looking speech bubbles and managing world state. If it needs a new character, it calls \`createCharacter('name', 'description')\` and keeps going.

But that tool then triggers a side brain piggy backing off the main cache that actually **creates** the node in the DB, and builds the image prompt, and all that.

I haven't set up the LLC and the stripe and all that, but I plan to start selling this... eventually. I DMed you a $1 link. I don't want my account pinged for advertising :|

SassyTest -- SillyTavern -- ST? Right? whatever. I've been working on this. Like. Hard.

comments.author: ProperDepartment
comments.body:
Wheel of Time showrunners on Prime just pretended they didn't kill off characters in the first season.

Maybe you can get away with it too lol.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Ha, "the showrunners did it first" is a defense I hadn't considered.

comments.author: playtetramental
comments.body: The most beneficial part of writing for me was design documents. I ended up with design documents about double the length of a novel I wrote with AI. For a dynamic world, you’d end up with player-specific design documents, and you’d have to get really, really good at organizing.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Per-player documents is pretty much what the saved state turns into, and keeping it organized is the hard part. Did you split yours by character or by plot thread?

replies.author: playtetramental
replies.body:
Nice on save states being per-player docs! 

Yeah, organization emerged over time for me. I spent almost the whole year refining it and creating new documents out of necessity. I created docs for characters, character voices (how they speak - this became large enough to be its own), locations, reader-knowledge, spells, schedules, prose-style, worldbuilding (how things come together), and outline.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Voices needing its own doc tracks, how someone talks is usually the first thing to drift. Reader-knowledge as a separate doc is a smart one, I'd guess that's what keeps reveals from leaking early.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color
comments.body:
I don't think we are there yet technically.

The only way I can make it work is to set it up with conventional systems running as a framework and use LLM as an overlay with several filters.

For instance with characters, you'll make a list of existing characters and the llm can pick from this list. I wouldn't try to rely on LLM to generate freely, I mean.. I would, and I have, but have determined that this will not hold up in long or big context.

I think we are many years out from running systems by LLM that involve more than user and agent in single conversation mode.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Picking from a list is close to where I landed for characters too. What I still want to keep open is what the player can try, even if everything that comes out of it gets checked against the fixed stuff.

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
Yeah, the more I've worked with it. I've gone back to conventional design and only have llm form the sentence and personality.

I ended up making a list of "action" and subcategories (such as movement etc), to be able to handle it properly. It's not as easy as one first thinks because of context size and drift of llm. I had to give items an "ownership" for instance

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Ownership on items is a good example, who's holding the key right now is exactly the kind of thing that drifts if it only lives in the text. Does the action list ever feel too narrow for what players actually type?

comments.author: Academic-Bench-8828
comments.body: You should try to put an interface between the llm and the rest of your game. Instead of having the llm try to remember everything, make some sort of out of context memory database.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Yeah, that's the direction. The storing part turned out to be the easy half, deciding which few facts to hand back on a given turn is where I keep getting it wrong.

replies.author: Academic-Bench-8828
replies.body: If I were you, I might consider an ECS architecture coupled with rotjs for it's scheduling algorithms. You can't expect the llm to remember everything, it will forget eventually. So make every prompt fresh - do not maintain a long chat. Clear it's chat history after every turn, you just need to make sure you are providing the history of the game in a compressed form.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Fresh prompt every turn is where I ended up too. Hadn't thought about borrowing a roguelike scheduler for turn order though, that's an interesting angle.

comments.author: Robonotes1760
comments.body: I suspect that the best architecture is to get the AI to write a traditional deterministic RPG and add specific constrained layers for the AI to generate.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: That's probably the safest version. I'd just miss the part where someone types a thing no rule anticipated and the game still rolls with it.

comments.author: DRAMAGO_Official
comments.body:
I'm on the DRAMAGO Worlds team, and this is the problem we've been sitting with as well.

We're building a persistent world, DEADWOOD, set in 1989. Players pick an identity, follow a main quest of about 15 to 20 turns, then the town opens up. The world is supposed to remember what you did, and it keeps moving even while you're away. So a single turn of writing was never the main worry. The worry is continuity: if you helped someone, crossed someone, or left something unfinished, that has to still matter the next time you run into them, or when you come back later.

We don't treat "keep everything in the context window" or "summarize until it fits" as the real goal. The question we keep coming back to is: what should still be able to change the next encounter? A past event only earns its place if it can change a relationship, close off a path, or make the town feel like it noticed you. The hardest cases are the early setups the player never comes back to. If they stay in the window forever, they drown the present. If they disappear, the world feels like it has no memory. I don't want to oversell a method we haven't settled on.

For people further along: how do you decide that something is still "live" after dozens of turns, especially things the player started early and then ignored?

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: I'd tie it to who or what could bring it back, not to how old it is. An early setup the player ignored stays quiet until they're near the person or place it belongs to, and then it gets a chance to matter again.
